opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that the cost of attacking goes way down, and that changes the economics of defense more than any single new technique does.

Historically, a lot of security has quietly relied on the fact that skilled attackers are scarce. Finding a novel vulnerability in a complex codebase, writing a reliable exploit, crafting a convincing spear-phishing campaign: all of that took real expertise and real hours. So defenders could get away with being a little behind, because attackers had to prioritize. They went after the high-value targets, and everyone else benefited from being uninteresting.

AI erodes that. If models can do a meaningful fraction of the work of a competent security researcher, then the long tail of targets that nobody bothered with before suddenly becomes worth attacking. Your obscure internal service, your small vendor with access to your systems, the legacy code nobody has looked at in ten years: those become reachable at scale. Social engineering gets cheaper and more personalized too. Anything that relied on "the attacker probably won't put in that much effort" is a weaker assumption now.

The encouraging part is that the same capabilities are available to defenders, and I'd argue defenders can benefit even more if they move first. You can point models at your own code and find bugs before anyone else does. You can do continuous review instead of the annual pentest. You can triage alerts that would otherwise drown a security team. Defense has always had more surface area to cover than offense, and that's exactly the kind of problem where cheap, scalable intelligence helps.

So the demand on defense is really about speed and coverage. You have to assume your attack surface is being examined much more thoroughly than before, and you need to examine it yourself at least as thoroughly, continuously, and with automation. The organizations that treat AI as a core part of their security program will be in good shape. The ones that wait until they see it used against them are going to have a rough few years.

r001.rationale: It says AI lowers the cost of attacking and can perform a meaningful fraction of a security researcher’s work, making offensive activity easier to scale.

r002.rationale: It links greater attack pressure to faster, broader, continuous, automated defense, but does not clearly say defense needs to become more agentic.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that AI changes defense less by introducing some brand-new category of threat and more by compressing the timelines everyone has gotten used to.

For a long time, the implicit assumption in defense was that attackers were resource-constrained. Finding a vulnerability took skilled people, writing an exploit took more skilled people, and tailoring a phishing campaign to a specific organization took real effort. That friction was doing a lot of quiet work for defenders. It meant most organizations were attacked by the lowest-effort version of an attacker, and you could get pretty far by just not being the easiest target.

What's changing is that models are getting genuinely good at the labor-intensive parts. Reading a large codebase and spotting where the logic is wrong, chaining together a few small bugs into something that matters, writing convincing communication in someone's voice. None of that is science fiction anymore. So the cost curve for attackers bends down, and the "don't be the easiest target" strategy stops being enough, because the floor rises for everyone.

The flip side, and I think people underweight this, is that the same capabilities are at least as useful for defense, and arguably more so. Defenders have an advantage attackers don't: they own the environment. They can read their own code, instrument their own systems, and run a model over every commit before it ships rather than after. The question of whether a model can find a vulnerability is symmetric. The question of who gets to run it first over a given piece of software is not, and defenders get to go first if they choose to.

So the demand I'd emphasize is speed and continuity. Patching on a quarterly cycle, or doing a pen test once a year, was already shaky. It becomes untenable when the time between a bug existing and someone finding it collapses. Defense has to become something that runs constantly, in the background, at the pace of the codebase itself. That's a tooling and process problem more than a research problem, and it's where I'd expect the most leverage over the next few years.

The other shift is in what you're defending against. As more real work gets delegated to agents, the attack surface starts to include the agents themselves. Someone who can get text in front of your model can try to steer it. That's a new kind of trust boundary, and most organizations haven't thought about it yet. I'd put a lot of weight on getting the fundamentals right there, least privilege for agents, clear separation between instructions and data, and treating everything a model reads from the outside world as untrusted by default.

If I had to compress it: the threats get faster, the defenses can get faster too, and the organizations that win are the ones who stop treating security as a periodic audit and start treating it as something that runs continuously alongside everything else they build.

r001.rationale: The response says models make labor-intensive offensive tasks easier and lower attackers’ costs, making attacks more capable and accessible.

r002.rationale: It says faster threats require continuous defense, but does not say defense needs to become more agentic or connect AI-driven threat pressure to that change.

astra-6.text:
I think AI changes both the scale of the threat and the speed at which you have to respond. An attacker can use AI to look for vulnerabilities, write code, and tailor attacks much more cheaply. So defenders have to be prepared for a world where there are a lot more attempts, and those attempts are more sophisticated.

That means defense has to become more automated, too. You can’t have a person manually investigate every alert. You want AI helping you understand what’s happening, identify the important signals, and respond quickly—with appropriate controls around actions that could disrupt your systems.

The opportunity is that defenders know things attackers don’t: how their systems are configured, what normal activity looks like, and what they’re trying to protect. AI can help them use that context. But you have to actually integrate it into the way you operate. Just having access to a capable model isn’t enough.

r001.rationale: It says attackers can use AI to find vulnerabilities, write code, and tailor attacks more cheaply, making offensive work easier.

r002.rationale: It describes more numerous and sophisticated AI-enabled attacks, then says defense must become more automated, with AI helping identify signals and respond quickly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI is going to make cybersecurity much more of a machine-speed problem. Today, a lot of attacks are limited by the time and expertise it takes to find a vulnerability and exploit it. As those capabilities become more automated, defenders will have to respond much faster.

The opportunity is that AI can help on defense, too: reviewing code, finding vulnerabilities, patching them, and making sense of the enormous volume of security alerts. But that requires more than an assistant that gives advice. You need systems that can take action, with appropriate controls, and you need to know how well they actually work. The big question is whether we can use these tools to close vulnerabilities faster than attackers can exploit them.

r001.rationale: It says AI will automate finding vulnerabilities and exploiting them, reducing the time and expertise attacks require.

r002.rationale: It describes attacks becoming faster through automation and says defenders need systems that can take action, establishing increased threat pressure as a reason for more agentic defense.
